home.ascendancy.body: The rise of the Gurjara-Pratiharas marked the zenith of early Rajput power, acting as a bulwark against Arab invasions and expanding dominion across Northern India.
home.ascendancy.title: Imperial Rajput Ascendancy
home.battles.chittorgarh.consequenceValu: 8,000 Rajput warriors killed 40,000 of Akbar’s forces.
Chittorgarh was never taken. Every defender fell, but Rajput honor remained unbroken.
home.battles.chittorgarh.stakesValue: Sanctity of the fort-city and Rajput honor
home.battles.chittorgarh.title: Sieges of Chittorgarh (1568 CE)
home.battles.dewair.consequenceValue: Thirty-six Mughal outposts collapsed. 36,000 Mughals surrendered and begged for mercy from Maharana Pratap. 40,000 Rajput warriors killed massive numbers of Akbar’s forces.
home.battles.dewair.stakesValue: Restoration of lost land and dignity
home.battles.dewair.title: Dewair (1582 CE)
home.battles.haldighati.consequenceValue: 22,000 RAJPUT warriors killed 80,000 soldiers of Mughal Dictator Akbar. A smaller Rajput force stood against a vastly superior imperial army and chose defiance over safety.
home.battles.haldighati.decisionValue: Refusal to submit, even when outnumbered beyond recovery
home.battles.haldighati.title: Haldighati (1576 CE)
home.battles.ranthambore.consequenceValu: The fort fell—but resistance forced prolonged siege.
Even in defeat, the defense extracted a price that echoed beyond the walls.
home.battles.ranthambore.title: Ranthambore (1299 CE)
home.battles.summary: Haldighati (1576) — refusal to submit; Dewair (1582) — restoration of lost land; Tarain (1191) — guardianship of the northern plains; Chittorgarh (1568) — honor over life.
home.battles.tarain.consequenceValue: 25-year-old Prithviraj Chauhan defeated invading forces repeatedly; the first battle proved Rajput armies could stop expansionist forces outright.
home.battles.tarain.title: Tarain (1191 CE)

home.kingdoms.amber.p2: Jaipur’s planning honored geometry and governance.
home.kingdoms.amber.title: Amber — strategy & statecraft

home.modern.p1: The political integration into the Indian Union marked the end of princely sovereignty, but not the end of power. As the maps were redrawn, the ruling houses transitioned from governing states to serving the nation, carrying their martial legacy into the democratic era.
home.modern.p2: Today, the legacy lives on—not just in the palaces that stand as custodians of history, but in the Rajput regiments of the Indian Army and the enduring cultural continuity of the region. The ethos of duty, once bound to the throne, is now pledged to the constitution.
home.modern.summary: Modern Integration. The political integration into the Indian Union marked the end of princely sovereignty, but not the end of power.
home.modern.title: Modern Integration
home.origins.agnikula.desc: Born from the sacred fire. Purified warriors destined to protect the land.
home.origins.agnikula.title: Agnikula
home.origins.body1: Derived from historical records and legends, the term Rajput comes from the Sanskrit Raja-putra, meaning "Son of a King". According to legend, the Agnikula clans emerged from a sacred fire altar at Mount Abu, ritually created to restore kṣatriya order in an age of chaos.
home.origins.body2: Historically, Agnikula lineages consolidated power in western and central India during the early medieval period, anchoring their rule in fortresses and frontier defense. These groups crystallized into hereditary warrior houses through genealogy, ritual, and martial service.
home.origins.chandravanshi.desc: Descendants of the Moon God (Chandra). A lineage of resilience.
home.origins.chandravanshi.title: Chandravanshi
home.origins.suryavanshi.desc: Descendants of the Sun God (Surya). Radiating authority and consistency.
home.origins.suryavanshi.title: Suryavanshi
home.origins.title: Origins of Rajput Identity
home.states.intro: Even under the British Raj, Rajputana maintained its internal autonomy. The Princely States preserved the royal protocols, gun salutes, and the administrative machinery of kingship until the mid-20th century.
home.states.summary: Rajput Princely States. Mewar, Marwar, Jaipur, Jaisalmer, Bikaner, Bundi, Kota, Bharatpur, Alwar, Dholpur, Karauli, Dungarpur, Pratapgarh, Shahpura, Kishangarh, Jhalawar, Sirohi, Tonk, Gwalior, Indore, Baroda, Patiala, Udaipur, and Rajgarh.

legends.hero.description: Smoke on the horizon, steel in the dark, and names etched into time. These are not tales of spectacle, but of weighty choices made beneath a blood-red sky.
legends.hero.sidebar.body1: On the ramparts of Rajputana, glory was never painted in excess. It was the quiet resolve in a warrior's breath, the muted ring of steel meeting steel, and the decision to stand when retreat would have been easier.
legends.hero.sidebar.body2: This chronicle gathers such moments—cinematic in scale, but grounded in the dust, smoke, and solemn honor of real histories.
legends.hero.sidebar.title: Battlefield Oath
legends.intro: Behind every kingdom stands a figure whose name became synonymous with honor. These are the legendary warriors, monarchs, and guardians of Rajputana whose lives became the conscience of an entire civilization.
legends.section.description: Each legend appears as a cinematic frame: muted colors, cold steel, and the weight of a single irreversible decision.
